Champaign
sham-PANE
noun
From the Old French champagne, “open country,” from the Latin campania (campus, “a field”); hence flat, open, level ground without wood or hill. A KJV hapax; it has nothing to do with the wine of that name.

Biblical Definition

A champaign is open country — a flat, level plain, unbroken by wood or hill, where a man can see a long way and be seen. It occurs once in the KJV, and the place it marks matters: Moses points the people toward Gerizim and Ebal, “in the land of the Canaanites, which dwell in the champaign over against Gilgal, beside the plains of Moreh” (Deu 11:30). This is the geography of covenant. The people are about to cross Jordan; and the LORD appoints that when they come in they shall “put the blessing upon mount Gerizim, and the curse upon mount Ebal” (Deu 11:29). Joshua did it exactly: all Israel, elders and officers and judges, the stranger as well as the home-born, stood half over against Gerizim and half over against Ebal with the ark and the Levites between, and the blessings and the cursings of the law were read aloud in the open (Jos 8:33). At Gilgal in the same open country they had already kept the passover in the plains of Jericho (Jos 5:10). The champaign is the theatre God chose for this. A covenant is not made in a corner. The blessing and the curse were set before the whole nation on level ground where every eye could see the two mountains and every ear could hear the law — because God deals with His people openly, and the terms He offers are public terms, plainly told, with nothing hidden in the hills.

Webster 1828 Definition

Open, flat, level country without wood or hill; a plain. A KJV hapax, naming the open ground over against Gilgal.

CHAMPAIGN, a flat, open country; level ground; a plain without wood or hill.

From Old French champagne, from Latin campania, “field, open country.”

It has no relation to the wine that bears a like name.

A KJV hapax, occurring but once (Deu 11:30).

It names the open ground over against Gilgal, by Gerizim and Ebal.

Key Scripture

Deu 11:30 — "Are they not on the other side Jordan, by the way where the sun goeth down, in the land of the Canaanites, which dwell in the champaign over against Gilgal, beside the plains of Moreh?"

Deu 11:29 — "And it shall come to pass, when the LORD thy God hath brought thee in unto the land whither thou goest to possess it, that thou shalt put the blessing upon mount Gerizim, and the curse upon mount Ebal."

Jos 8:33 — "And all Israel, and their elders, and officers, and their judges, stood on this side the ark and on that side before the priests the Levites, which bare the ark of the covenant of the LORD, as well the stranger, as he that was born among them; half of them over against mount Gerizim, and half of them over against mount Ebal; as Moses the servant of the LORD had commanded before, that they should bless the people of Israel."

Jos 5:10 — "And the children of Israel encamped in Gilgal, and kept the passover on the fourteenth day of the month at even in the plains of Jericho."

Modern Corruption

Not a contested doctrine but the old word for open country; it recovers that God sets blessing and curse before His people in the open, on terms plainly told.

expand to see more

The word rebukes a religion of the private and the vague. The LORD did not whisper His covenant to a committee; He appointed the champaign, the open plain over against Gilgal, with two mountains standing up on either hand, and there the blessing and the curse were set before the whole nation. Joshua carried it out to the letter — all Israel, elders, officers, judges, the stranger as well as the home-born, the ark and the Levites in the midst, and the law read aloud so that not a word was left out. God’s dealings with His people are open dealings. The terms are published; the blessing and the curse are both named; and no man on that plain could plead afterward that he had not been told.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the plainness of God’s covenant terms. Level ground is honest ground: nothing hides in a champaign. If the LORD had meant to save on undisclosed conditions He would not have staged the reading between Gerizim and Ebal, where every eye saw both mountains at once. Blessing on the one hand for obedience; curse on the other for rebellion — and the gospel does not soften that arithmetic but satisfies it, for Christ was made a curse for us, hanging on a tree between heaven and earth in the open, that the blessing of Abraham might come on the Gentiles. The two mountains still stand. The Lamb has stood under one of them for His people.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means open, flat, level country — a plain without wood or hill.

expand to see more

Champaign — Old French champagne, “open country.”

From the Latin campania, from campus, “a field.”

It denotes flat, level ground, unbroken by wood or hill.

It bears no relation to the wine of the like name.

A KJV hapax, naming the plain over against Gilgal (Deu 11:30).

Usage

"The Canaanites dwelt in the champaign over against Gilgal — open, level, unhidden ground."

"God set the blessing and the curse in the champaign, where every eye could see both mountains."

"Nothing hides in a champaign: the covenant terms were published, not whispered."
